facts.statement: The scientific name of the animal is Megalneusaurus.
facts.quote: taxon: Megalneusaurus

facts.statement: The genus Megalneusaurus was described by Wilbur Clinton Knight in 1898.
facts.quote: authority: Knight, 1898

facts.statement: The type species of the genus is Megalneusaurus rex.
facts.quote: type_species: Megalneusaurus rex

facts.statement: Cimoliosaurus rex is a synonym for Megalneusaurus rex.
facts.quote: synonyms: Cimoliosaurus rex Knight, 1895

facts.statement: Megalneusaurus is a large pliosaurid plesiosaur from the Late Jurassic of North America.
facts.quote: Megalneusaurus is a genus of large pliosaurid plesiosaur from the Late Jurassic of North America.

facts.statement: Wilbur Clinton Knight first described the animal as a species of Cimoliosaurus in 1895 before elevating it to its own genus in 1898.
facts.quote: It was provisionally described as a species of Cimoliosaurus by the geologist Wilbur Clinton Knight in 1895, before being given its own genus by the same author in 1898.

facts.statement: The only known species, M. rex, is known from specimens found mainly in the Redwater Shale Member of the Sundance Formation in Wyoming, United States.
facts.quote: The only known species is M. rex, known from several specimens mainly found in the Redwater Shale Member, within the Sundance Formation, Wyoming, United States.

facts.statement: A specimen from the Naknek Formation in southern Alaska was referred to the genus in 1994.
facts.quote: A specimen discovered in the Naknek Formation in southern Alaska was referred to the genus in 1994.

facts.statement: Some paleontologists consider the genus dubious due to the loss of most fossils, while others maintain its validity.
facts.quote: The loss of most fossils has led some paleontologists to consider the genus as dubious, although its validity is maintained by many authors.

facts.statement: Megalneusaurus likely had four flippers, a short tail, an elongated head, and a short neck, suggesting it was a thalassophonean-like pliosaurid.
facts.quote: Like some other plesiosaurs, Megalneusaurus have four flippers, a short tail, and most likely an elongated head and short neck, suggesting that it is a thalassophonean-like pliosaurid.

facts.statement: The rear flippers of Megalneusaurus were larger than the front flippers.
facts.quote: The rear flippers were larger than those at the front.

facts.statement: Megalneusaurus used its flippers for a swimming method known as subaqueous flight.
facts.quote: Like other plesiosaurs, Megalneusaurus was well-adapted to aquatic life, using its flippers for a method of swimming known as subaqueous flight.

facts.statement: Based on stomach contents, Megalneusaurus fed on cephalopods and fish, though it may have also eaten contemporary plesiosaurs.
facts.quote: Based on stomach contents, the animal fed on cephalopods and fish, although it could also have fed on contemporary plesiosaurs.

facts.statement: The Alaskan specimen suggests that Megalneusaurus occupied colder waters with less diverse fauna.
facts.quote: The Alaskan specimen also indicates that it would have occupied colder waters, where the fauna was less diverse.

facts.statement: Wilbur Clinton Knight discovered the fossils near the town of Ervay, Wyoming, in 1895.
facts.quote: In 1895, geologist Wilbur Clinton Knight went to examine an oil field near the small town of Ervay, Wyoming, USA.

facts.statement: Knight initially named the specimen Cimoliosaurus rex, provisionally classifying it pending a more detailed description.
facts.quote: He therefore named a new species of Cimoliosaurus, C. rex, to which he provisionally classified it pending a more in-depth description.

facts.statement: In 1898, Knight described the specimen in detail and named the genus Megalneusaurus, making the species M. rex.
facts.quote: It was three years later, in 1898, that Knight described the specimen in more detail and named the distinct genus Megalneusaurus to include it, the species thus becoming M. rex.

facts.statement: The fossils first unearthed by Knight are now held at the University of Wyoming, catalogued as UW 4602.
facts.quote: The fossils of the pliosaur first unearthed by Knight have since been sent to the University of Wyoming, where they are catalogued as UW 4602.

facts.statement: The type locality was found in the summer of 1996, aided by letters and a map drawn by Knight in 1901.
facts.quote: It was during the summer of 1996 that the type locality was finally found, thanks among other things to letters and especially a map drawn by Knight in 1901.

facts.statement: The type locality is in the Redwater Shale Member of the upper Sundance Formation, dating to the Oxfordian stage of the Late Jurassic.
facts.quote: The site is located at the Redwater Shale Member of the upper part of the Sundance Formation, which dates to the Oxfordian stage of the Late Jurassic.

facts.statement: Fossils possibly belonging to two other specimens of Megalneusaurus have been reported.
facts.quote: Fossils coming possibly from two other specimens of Megalneusaurus have also been reported.

facts.statement: Two bone fragments of Megalneusaurus were collected in 1922 by prospector Jack Mason and received by W. R. Smith of the United States Geological Survey.
facts.quote: In 1922, W. R. Smith of the United States Geological Survey received two bone fragments from prospector Jack Mason.

facts.statement: A Megalneusaurus specimen from southern Alaska dates to the Oxfordian and Kimmeridgian stages of the Late Jurassic.
facts.quote: The stratigraphic unit in which this specimen was discovered corresponds to the Snug Harbor Siltstone Member of the Naknek Formation, dating from between the Oxfordian and Kimmeridgian stages of the Late Jurassic.

facts.statement: Weems and Blodgett initially classified the Alaskan specimen as Megalneusaurus sp. because they were uncertain if it belonged to M. rex or another species.
facts.quote: However, as their description and comparison is only based on an isolated bone, they referred it under the name Megalneusaurus sp., the authors being uncertain as to whether the specimen belonged to M. rex or another species.

facts.statement: Wahl and colleagues reclassified the Alaskan specimen as M. rex in 2010, though some authors remain doubtful about its attribution to the genus.
facts.quote: Although some authors have been doubtful about the attribution of this specimen to the genus in later works, Wahl and colleagues reclassified this specimen as an M. rex in 2010, but considered the bone to be a partial propodial.

facts.statement: Megalneusaurus belongs to the large-headed, short-necked pliosauromorph morphotype.
facts.quote: Megalneusaurus belonging to the latter category.

facts.statement: Most recent estimates suggest Megalneusaurus was between 7.6 and 9.2 meters long.
facts.quote: However, most recent estimates reduce the size of Megalneusaurus to between 7.6 and 9.2 m long.

facts.statement: In 2024, Ruizhe Jackevan Zhao estimated Megalneusaurus to be approximately 9.8 meters long with a body mass of 12 tons.
facts.quote: In 2024, Chinese paleontologist Ruizhe Jackevan Zhao suggested that Megalneusaurus would have been similar in size to Pliosaurus funkei, which according to his model was approximately 9.8 m long with a body mass of 12 t.

facts.statement: The Alaskan Megalneusaurus specimen is smaller than the holotype, though no specific size estimate has been provided for it.
facts.quote: The referred specimen from Alaska is smaller in measurement than the holotype specimen, although no estimate of its size has been given.

facts.statement: Knight initially identified the flippers of the holotype specimen as hind limbs in 1895.
facts.quote: When Knight reported the discovery of the holotype specimen in 1895, he initially identified the flippers as hind limbs.

facts.statement: The discovery of a third flipper in 2008 confirmed that the initial identification of the flippers as hind limbs was correct.
facts.quote: The discovery of the third flipper in 2008, however, confirms that the first identification was correct (as previously suggested by McHenry), as it was 15% smaller than those first discovered.

facts.statement: Megalneusaurus had longer hind limbs than forelimbs, consistent with other pliosaurids.
facts.quote: This also confirms that Megalneusaurus has longer hind limbs than forelimbs, like other pliosaurids.

facts.statement: The humerus of Megalneusaurus was estimated to be 85% the length of the femur.
facts.quote: The humerus would have been smaller than the femur, with estimates suggesting that the bone would have reached only 85% of the latter's length.

facts.statement: Knight concluded in 1898 that the fossils belonged to a pliosaur, comparing them to Pliosaurus and Peloneustes.
facts.quote: However, the same author concluded that the fossils belonged to a pliosaur in 1898, comparing it to the pliosaurids Pliosaurus and Peloneustes, although he also noted the anatomical resemblance with the plesiosaurid Plesiosaurus.

facts.statement: In 2003, Ellis noted that many researchers doubted the diagnostic value of the holotype due to lost fossils, while others held the opposite opinion.
facts.quote: In 2003, Ellis mentioned that many researchers doubted the diagnostic nature of the holotype specimen due to the loss of the previously mentioned fossils, although he also points out that some are of the opposite opinion.

facts.statement: Benson and Druckenmiller named the clade Thalassophonea within Pliosauridae in 2013.
facts.quote: In 2013, British paleontologist Roger B. J. Benson and his American colleague Patrick S. Druckenmiller named a new clade within Pliosauridae, Thalassophonea.

facts.statement: Megalneusaurus swam using a method known as subaqueous flight, using its flippers as hydrofoils.
facts.quote: Plesiosaurs such as Megalneusaurus employed a method of swimming known as subaqueous flight, using their flippers as hydrofoils.

facts.statement: Wahl and colleagues proposed in 2010 that the rear flippers of the holotype had an aspect ratio of 8.0 and the front flippers had an aspect ratio of at least 8.2.
facts.quote: In 2010, Wahl and colleagues proposed that the rear flippers of the holotype specimen have aspect ratios of 8.0, while the front flippers would have aspect ratios of at least 8.2.

facts.statement: The high aspect ratios of Megalneusaurus flippers suggest it could move quickly and nimbly, albeit inefficiently, to capture prey.
facts.quote: These ratios, surpassing those of other pliosauromorphs, seem to indicate that Megalneusaurus would probably have been able to move quickly and nimbly, albeit inefficiently, in order to capture prey.

facts.statement: Megalneusaurus likely fed on contemporary plesiosaurs, particularly juveniles or subadults.
facts.quote: Being a large pliosaurid, Megalneusaurus would likely have fed on other contemporary plesiosaurs, particularly juveniles or subadults.

facts.statement: Massare and colleagues interpreted Megalneusaurus as an opportunistic apex predator in the Sundance Formation in 2014.
facts.quote: Despite the lack of direct evidence of interactions, Megalneusaurus is interpreted as an opportunistic apex predator in the Sundance Formation according to Judy A. Massare and colleagues in 2014.

facts.statement: Researchers in 2003 found that the hind limbs of the Megalneusaurus rex holotype suffered from avascular necrosis.
facts.quote: According to Bruce M. Rothschild and Glenn W. Storrs in 2003, the hind limbs of the M. rex holotype specimen are affected by avascular necrosis.

facts.statement: Scientists suggest the avascular necrosis in Megalneusaurus resulted from ascending too quickly after deep dives.
facts.quote: This is the result of ascending too quickly after a deep diving.

facts.statement: Megalneusaurus fossils are found in Oxfordian-aged rocks of the Redwater Shale Member of the Sundance Formation.
facts.quote: Megalneusaurus comes from the Oxfordian-aged (Upper Jurassic) rocks of the Redwater Shale Member of the Sundance Formation.

facts.statement: When Megalneusaurus lived, the Sundance Sea where it inhabited was mostly less than 40 meters deep.
facts.quote: When Megalneusaurus was alive, most of the Sundance Sea was less than 40 m deep.

facts.statement: An Alaskan specimen of Megalneusaurus likely comes from Oxfordian to Kimmeridgian rocks of the Snug Harbor Siltstone Member of the Naknek Formation.
facts.quote: The Alaskan specimen of Megalneusaurus likely originates from Oxfordian to Kimmeridgian rocks of the Snug Harbor Siltstone Member of the Naknek Formation.

facts.statement: The region where the Alaskan Megalneusaurus specimen was found was at a paleolatitude of over 60°N, creating a boreal environment.
facts.quote: When the specimen was alive, this region was located at a paleolatitude of more than 60°N, making the area a boreal environment.
